questions.prompt: Given `void f(int, double);` and `void f(double, int);`, what happens at the call site `f(1, 2);`?
options: Calls `f(int, double)` because the first parameter is an exact match.
Ill-formed due to ambiguity because each candidate is strictly better on one argument and worse on the other.
Calls `f(double, int)` because the second parameter converts last.
Calls whichever overload was declared earlier in the translation unit.
questions.explanation: Under `[over.match.best]`, a winner must be at least as good on *all* arguments and strictly better on at least one. On `f(1, 2)`, the first overload wins argument 1 (`int` exact vs `int->double`), while the second wins argument 2, resulting in an ambiguity error.

questions.prompt: Given `void g(int);` and `void g(double) = delete;`, what happens when calling `g(2.5)`?
options: Calls `g(int)` by truncating `2.5` to `2` because the deleted overload is skipped during viability.
Ambiguous between `g(int)` and `g(double)`.
Compile error: `g(double)` wins overload resolution and is then rejected as deleted.
Undefined behavior at runtime.
questions.explanation: Deleted functions participate in Phase 1 and Phase 2 of overload resolution just like ordinary functions (`[dcl.fct.def.delete]`). Because `2.5` (`double`) is an exact match for `g(double)`, overload resolution selects `g(double)` and then diagnoses the call to a deleted function.

questions.prompt: Given `int log(bool);` and `int log(const std::string&);`, which overload does `log("hello")` invoke?
options: `log(bool)`, because array-to-pointer plus pointer-to-boolean is a Standard Conversion Sequence.
`log(const std::string&)`, because `"hello"` is text.
Ambiguous, because both `bool` and `std::string` require one conversion step.
Ill-formed, because string literals cannot convert to `bool`.
questions.explanation: In `[over.ics.rank]/2`, *every* Standard Conversion Sequence strictly outranks *every* User-Defined Conversion Sequence. Turning `const char[6]` into `bool` (array-to-pointer + boolean conversion) is purely a Standard Conversion, defeating `std::string(const char*)`.

questions.prompt: Given `int pick(const int&);` and `template <class T> int pick(T&);`, what does `int x = 10; pick(x);` return?
options: `1`, because non-template functions always beat function templates.
Compile error: ambiguous between `const int&` and `T&`.
`1`, because `const int&` is preferred for scalar types.
`2`, because `int&` has a strictly better reference-binding conversion than `const int&`, before template tie-breaking runs.
questions.explanation: Overload resolution compares conversion sequences *before* applying the non-template-vs-template tie-breaker (`[over.match.best]/2`). Binding mutable lvalue `x` to `int&` (deduced from `T&`) is strictly better than binding to `const int&` (`[over.ics.rank]/3.2.6`), so the template wins.

questions.prompt: Why does declaring both `void h(int);` and `void h(const int&);` make the call `h(5)` ambiguous?
options: `const int&` cannot bind to a prvalue literal `5`.
Both `int` (identity/Exact Match) and `const int&` (Exact Match binding a materialized temporary) have indistinguishable conversion ranks.
By-value `int` always ranks lower than reference parameters.
Only `h(const int&)` is viable for literals.
questions.explanation: Under `[over.best.ics]` and `[over.ics.rank]`, passing a prvalue `5` to `int` is an Identity Exact Match, and binding it to `const int&` is also an Exact Match with no distinguishing sub-rank difference against a non-reference parameter. Neither sequence is better, so the call is ambiguous.

questions.prompt: In C++20 and C++23, why does `7 != Key{7}` compile when `Key` only defines `friend bool operator==(const Key&, int);`?
options: The compiler generates an implicit conversion from `int` to `Key` automatically.
Friend declarations inject free operators for both argument orders automatically.
`[over.match.oper]` synthesizes rewritten `!=` and reversed `operator==` candidates during overload resolution.
Because `Key` is an aggregate, `!=` performs memberwise comparison.
questions.explanation: In C++20 (`[over.match.oper]/3`), an expression `a != b` considers rewritten candidates `!(a == b)` and `!(b == a)` synthesized from viable `operator==` overloads, allowing `7 != Key{7}` to resolve to `!(Key{7} == 7)` without writing boilerplate reverse overloads.
